h1: Citra, Mosaic and Simcoe in Indian IPAs
title: Citra, Mosaic and Simcoe in Indian IPAs | Craft Beer School
desc: How to use Citra, Mosaic and Simcoe in an IPA brewed in India: what each hop brings, dose rates, whirlpool and dry hop timing and keeping them fresh.
teaser: Three American hops built the modern IPA. Using them well in India is mostly about freshness, timing and not wasting expensive pellets.
standfirst: Citra, Mosaic and Simcoe are three of the most widely used aroma hops in modern IPAs. Each brings something different. In India, where every kilogram is imported, getting value from them depends on cold storage, addition timing and dry hop technique as much as on the recipe.
sections: Each hop brings a different part of the IPA

All three are high-alpha American aroma varieties, typically around 11 to 14% alpha acid. That makes them usable for bittering too, though most brewers save them for late additions.

  • Simcoe, released in 2000, gives pine, passion fruit and a resinous, slightly earthy edge. Some lots carry a catty note that tasters either like or do not.
  • Citra, released in 2008, is the bright one: grapefruit, lime, lychee and tropical fruit. It is high in myrcene and also carries linalool and geraniol.
  • Mosaic, released in 2012 and bred from Simcoe, adds blueberry, mango and tropical fruit over a piney base.

Used together, Simcoe gives structure, Citra gives brightness and Mosaic fills the middle. Plenty of excellent IPAs use only one or two of them.
Late additions get the most from every gram

Hop oils evaporate in a rolling boil. A Citra addition at 60 minutes adds bitterness but almost none of the aroma you paid for. Put most of these hops in the whirlpool and the dry hop.

A practical split for a 1,000 litre West Coast style IPA at around 6.5% ABV:

  • Bittering: a neutral high-alpha hop or extract to about 40 IBU.
  • Whirlpool: 2 to 4 g/L of the trio at 75 to 80 °C, rested 20 to 30 minutes. Our guide to whirlpool hopping covers temperature and time.
  • Dry hop: 5 to 8 g/L, split across one or two additions.

Hazy IPAs often run dry hop rates well above 10 g/L. Above that range the returns fall and grassy, vegetal flavours can creep in.
Dry hop timing changes the result

Dry hopping during active fermentation encourages biotransformation. Yeast can convert some hop compounds, such as geraniol from Citra, into others with different aromas. Dry hopping after fermentation, at lower temperature, tends to give a cleaner, greener hop character.

Either way, watch for hop creep. Hops carry small amounts of enzymes that break down dextrins into fermentable sugar. Yeast then restarts, raising the ABV, dropping the gravity and sometimes producing diacetyl. Our guide to hop creep explains how to manage it. Hold the beer warm for a few days after dry hopping and check for diacetyl before you crash it.

Every kilogram of these hops is imported, usually as T-90 pellets in nitrogen-flushed foil packs. They are expensive, so losses hurt. Heat is the main enemy. A box left on a warm loading bay for an afternoon loses aroma you cannot get back.

Store packs frozen, ideally below 0 °C. Once opened, flush with CO2, reseal tightly and use within a few weeks. Order in quantities you can use within a few months. Check the hop storage index on every certificate.
Adjunct grists can show hops more clearly

Many Indian breweries already use rice in their lagers. A small share of rice or flaked maize in an IPA, around 10 to 15%, lightens the body and dries the finish. That can make the hop aroma stand out more. Our guide to rice and maize adjuncts in India covers how to cook and mash them. Keep the malt base clean and pale so the hops do the talking.

Water matters too. A sulphate to chloride ratio leaning towards sulphate sharpens hop bitterness and makes a West Coast style IPA taste crisper. Hazy styles usually lean the other way, towards chloride, for a softer palate.
Freshness at the bar decides what drinkers taste

Hop aroma fades fast in warm conditions. An IPA that tastes vivid at the brewery can taste dull and sweet after two weeks in a warm warehouse. Brewery-fresh and cold all the way to the tap is the goal. Shorter shelf lives, cold storage and date coding all help. This is the floor detail that matters most in India: the brewery controls the recipe, but the cold chain controls the beer.

Getting maximum aroma from expensive hops, without hop creep, oxidation or vegetal notes, depends on understanding hop chemistry and yeast interaction together. That is what turns a good IPA recipe into a consistent one.

Brew one small base IPA and split it into three fermenters. Dry hop each with one of the three varieties at the same rate. Taste them side by side with your team. You will learn more about what each hop gives your beer than any description can tell you.
faqs: Citra gives grapefruit, lime, lychee and tropical fruit aromas. It is one of the brightest and most citrus-forward American hops.
Yes. Mosaic was bred from Simcoe and shares some of its pine character, with added blueberry and tropical fruit.
How much dry hop should an IPA use?
Around 5 to 8 g/L is common for West Coast styles. Hazy IPAs often go above 10 g/L.
How should imported hops be stored in India?
Frozen, ideally below 0 °C, in sealed foil packs. Flush opened packs with CO2 and use them within a few weeks.
